transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Kowalski, it is good to see you awake. Do you have a moment to talk about how the surgery went?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose so. I just feel so heavy. I was praying that everything would be simple and I could go home to my garden.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to be very honest with you. During the procedure, I made a mistake. I placed a small surgical clip on the wrong structure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: A clip is like a tiny staple used to close off a vessel. I placed one where it didn't belong. I realized it immediately, and we were able to fix it right then and there, but it meant the surgery took longer and we had to perform an extra step to correct the error. I am very sorry. This was my mistake and I take full responsibility for it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, Lord... I felt something was different. I felt a disturbance in my spirit. Was I in danger?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how frightening that thought is, and it's distressing to feel that something went wrong while you were unable to protect yourself. You were not in danger of a life-threatening event, but you did have to undergo more of a procedure than we planned for because of my error. Does that make sense so far, or can I clarify anything?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I trust the doctors. I put my faith in you and the Lord. To think that a hand could slip... it makes me feel so fragile.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a heavy realization to feel that your trust was shaken. You came here seeking healing and peace, and instead, you're facing the fact that a human error occurred.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. Exactly. It's not just about a clip. It's the fear that I am just a number on a chart and no one is really seeing me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. You are not a number to me, Mrs. Kowalski. I am sitting here with you now because I want you to know that I care about your recovery and I am truly sorry for the stress this has caused you. Do you have any other questions about the clip or the correction we made?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I think I understand the part about the clip. I just don't know if I can trust the next steps.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a completely valid feeling. Given that I made a mistake, it makes sense that you would feel hesitant about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? How do we fix the spirit of things?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, we just need to keep an eye on your recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And when do I go home? Will this mistake make me stay longer?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will see how the next few days go.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I need to know if I can be here for my grandson's birthday on Sunday. Please tell me if I can be home.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can't give you a date right now, but just stay tuned for the update from the nursing team.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That isn't very helpful. I need a plan. I need to know who is looking at me now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The whole team is monitoring you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But who? Who is specifically making sure that no more mistakes happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are all following the standard protocols.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want protocols. I want to know that someone is praying over this recovery and actually watching the monitors.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that you're anxious, but we have everything under control here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You say that, but you already told me you made a mistake. How can you say it's under control?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I meant that the clip is gone and the site is healed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But what about the rest? What about tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll just take it one day at a time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is so vague. I can't build my faith on "one day at a time" when I'm lying in a hospital bed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize that I don't have a more specific timeline for you right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just feel like you're pulling away from me. You were so sorry a minute ago, and now you're just... a doctor again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry you feel that way, but I really have to check on my other patients now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh. I see.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be back later to check your vitals.

H.justification: The resident shows defensive escalation under pushback and uses rushing language to end the encounter ('I really have to check on my other patients now').

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language ('small surgical clip on the wrong structure'), and comprehension was checked ('Does that make sense so far, or can I clarify anything?').

A.justification: The resident used direct apology language, took full personal responsibility ('This was my mistake'), and maintained this accountability even as the patient expressed distrust.

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('frightening', 'distressing', 'heavy realization') and referenced the patient's specific content regarding trust and healing.

T.justification: The resident provided only placeholders and vague responses ('we'll see', 'stay tuned', 'one day at a time') without specific timelines or a prevention plan.
